strengths: The problem is well motivated. Figure 1 provides a clear analytical example showing why both contextual information and intervention-set selection can matter for achieving the optimal reward.

The hierarchical design is understandable. Averaging historical UCB values offers a plausible way to compare scopes before observing their contexts, and separating scope-selection regret from action-selection regret is useful.

The experiments report 110 seeds, 700 interventions, and uncertainty intervals. Using a common HEBO backend improves comparability, while the context, noise, and backend ablations provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The reduction from general mixed policies to the bandit model in Section B.1 is not justified. A compatible scope can require an action A before a context C affected by A, followed by another action conditioned on C. Algorithm 2 instead observes all context first and jointly selects all actions, assuming a fixed context distribution. This can violate both the permitted information dependencies and the causal sampling process. The paper needs to establish that retained POMPSs avoid this problem or restrict its claimed setting.

The central regret proof contains substantive gaps. On page 27, action regret is bounded by the range of f*(c) across contexts; this is false: f(x,c)=-xc on [0,1]^2 has f*(c)=0 but positive regret at x=1 and c>0. This invalidates the stated justification for the martingale bound. Additionally, Equation (21) and the subsequent derivation use c(T), containing worst-arm information gain, whereas the stated instance-dependent bound uses arm-averaged information gain in its leading term without justification. Theorem 1 is therefore not established as written.

The relationship between the theoretical and implemented algorithms is insufficiently explained. The analysis assumes independent GP draws with known kernels, compact domains, and independent Gaussian noise, while experiments use HEBO with learned transformations and SCMs that violate these assumptions. Figure 1, for example, produces action-dependent, non-Gaussian residuals. The guarantees should be clearly limited to the analyzed model, with the practical modifications separately specified.

The evaluation does not isolate the main algorithmic contribution. There is no comparison of the historical-UCB selector against uniform allocation or ordinary reward-based UCB over the same POMPSs. Functional Causal BO is discussed but not evaluated, and comparisons with model-based causal BO on compatible examples are missing. Much of the demonstrated advantage follows from giving the method a richer policy class or removing redundant variables.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported. Section 3 explicitly retains exponential brute-force scope enumeration. The example with 57 contextual and 29 intervenable variables contains only two POMPSs and mainly demonstrates dimensionality reduction. Enumeration timings and experiments varying the number of candidate scopes are needed to establish computational scalability.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the substantial experimental repetition. The supplied manuscript provides no location for the claimed public implementation and omits concrete experimental exploration schedules and acquisition-optimization settings. Benchmark equations also contain consequential inconsistencies: Appendix A.1.2 omits Cancer from the PSA equation but subsequently substitutes it, and Appendix A.3 defines C4 through itself. These prevent an unambiguous reconstruction of the evaluated environments.
